adonis: The beautiful youth of Greek myth, loved by Aphrodite, who died hunting a boar and was mourned each year.
akbar: The Mughal emperor who widened his realm across northern India by war and alliance and governed it through a court of mixed faiths.
akhenaten: The Egyptian pharaoh who moved his court to a new city at Amarna and set the sun disc above the other gods.
alfred-the-great: The West Saxon king who held out against the Danes, won at Edington and rebuilt his realm's defences and learning.
antigone: The Theban princess of Greek tragedy who defied her uncle's order to bury her brother and paid for it.
arachne: The Lydian weaver of Greek myth who challenged Athena to a contest of skill and was turned into a spider.
argus-panoptes: The hundred-eyed giant of Greek myth set by Hera to watch Io, since only some of his eyes ever slept at once.
asclepius: The Greek hero-physician, taught the healing arts by the centaur Chiron, honoured later at temples where the sick came to be cured.
aset: The Egyptian goddess Isis, who in Plutarch's telling searched the land for her slain husband and gathered him back together.
ashmantle: A fallen Watcher from the Book of 1 Enoch, one of the named members of that company.
ashurbanipal: The Assyrian king who gathered a vast library of clay tablets at Nineveh and was shown on reliefs hunting lions.
attila-the-hun: The king of the Huns who led his horsemen against both Roman empires in the mid-fifth century and marched deep into Gaul and Italy.
augustus: The heir of Julius Caesar who outlasted his rivals, ended Rome's civil wars and became its first emperor.
banquo-s-ghost: The murdered general's ghost in Shakespeare's Macbeth, who takes a seat at the royal feast and is seen only by the guilty king.
basilisk: The serpent-king of ancient and medieval natural histories, small but so deadly that its glance and breath were said to kill.
bjorn-ironside: The Viking leader of Norse tradition, a son of Ragnar Lothbrok, who raided widely and ruled in Sweden.
bloody-mary: The mirror ghost of folklore, said to appear in the glass when her name is chanted in a dark room.
brian-boru: The High King of Ireland who broke the power of the Vikings at Clontarf in 1014 and died in the fighting.
brutus: The Roman senator who joined the plot against Julius Caesar in 44 BC and later fought and died at Philippi.
caligula: A young Roman emperor whose short, erratic reign was famed for lavish spectacles and ended in his murder by his own guards.
calypso: The sea-nymph of Homer's Odyssey who kept Odysseus on her island for years before the gods ordered his release.
canute-the-great: The Danish prince who won the English throne in 1016 and ruled England, Denmark and Norway as a North Sea empire.
cao-cao: The warlord of the late Han who rose to rule northern China and laid the base for the state of Wei.
captain-nemo: The mysterious commander of the submarine Nautilus in Verne's novel, who roams the deep and fights a giant squid.
caracalla: The Roman emperor who fought on the northern frontier, granted citizenship to nearly all free men of the empire and was killed on campaign.
cato-the-younger: The Roman senator and Stoic who opposed Caesar to the end and took his own life at Utica rather than submit.
cesare-borgia: The Italian soldier-prince who carved out a state in the Romagna for his father, the pope, and was admired by Machiavelli.
charlemagne: The Frankish king who united much of western Europe by conquest and was crowned emperor in Rome on Christmas Day, 800.
charles-martel: The Frankish ruler who stopped the Umayyad army of al-Andalus at Tours in 732 and laid the ground for the Carolingian kings.
chernobog: The black god of old Slavic tradition, set against the white god in a pairing of dark and light.
ching-shih: The widow who commanded a vast pirate fleet off southern China in the early 1800s, then bargained her way to a peaceful retirement.
commodus: The Roman emperor who ruled after Marcus Aurelius and took to fighting in the arena before crowds, until his murder in 192.
crassus: The wealthiest man in Rome, who crushed Spartacus's revolt in 71 BC and later died leading a failed campaign against Parthia.
cyclopes: The one-eyed giants of Greek myth, smiths who forged Zeus's thunderbolts in Hesiod's account of the early world.
cyrano-de-bergerac: The big-nosed swordsman-poet, drawn from a real seventeenth-century duellist, who fought with blade and wit and wooed by proxy.
cyrus-the-great: The Persian king who overthrew the Medes, Lydia and Babylon and built the largest empire the world had yet seen.
daedalus: The master craftsman of Greek myth who built the labyrinth for King Minos and made wings to escape Crete.
darius-the-great: The Persian king who organised the empire into provinces, carved his deeds at Behistun and sent the expedition beaten at Marathon.
don-quixote: The gaunt gentleman of La Mancha who, steeped in tales of chivalry, rode out as a knight-errant and charged at windmills.
edward-i-longshanks: The tall English king who campaigned in Wales, built great castles there and fought William Wallace and the Scots for years.
erebus: The primordial darkness of Greek myth, born of Chaos in Hesiod's Theogony and father of Aether and Day.
erik-the-red: The Norse chieftain outlawed from Iceland who sailed west around 982 and founded the first settlements in Greenland.
eros-cupid: The winged archer of Greek and Roman myth whose arrows kindled love in gods and mortals alike.
francisco-pizarro: The Spanish conquistador who captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532 and went on to found Lima.
frederick-the-great: The Prussian king who made his small state a major power through the Silesian wars and the hard fighting of the Seven Years' War.
gaius-marius: The Roman general who opened the legions to landless men, beat the Germanic tribes and held the consulship seven times.
gargoyle: The carved stone monster perched on cathedral roofs to spout rain, and in Rouen's legend a dragon that once troubled the Seine.
ghoul: The grave-haunting creature of Arabian tales, a shape-changing desert dweller that lures travellers and feeds on the dead.
golem: A clay guardian of Prague folklore, shaped from river mud and woken to keep watch, then laid to rest.
gorgons: The three monstrous sisters of Greek myth with snakes for hair, whose gaze turned onlookers to stone, Medusa among them.
griffin: The lion-bodied creature with an eagle's head and wings, said by ancient writers to guard gold in the far east.
gustavus-adolphus: The Swedish king who reformed his army, led it through Germany in the Thirty Years' War and fell at Lutzen in 1632.
hadrian: The Roman emperor who toured the provinces, gave up lands beyond the frontier and built a great wall across northern Britain.
hammurabi: The king of Babylon who unified Mesopotamia in the eighteenth century BC and had a famous set of laws inscribed on a stone pillar.
harold-godwinson: The last Anglo-Saxon king of England, who beat the Norwegians at Stamford Bridge and then fell to the Normans at Hastings.
harpy: The winged storm-spirits of Greek myth who snatched away food and people, driven off by the Argonauts in their tale.
hayreddin-barbarossa: The Ottoman corsair who rose to admiral of the fleet and made the Mediterranean an Ottoman sea, winning at Preveza in 1538.
helen-of-troy: The Spartan queen whose departure with Paris to Troy set the Greeks sailing to war, as Homer's Iliad tells it.
henry-morgan: The Welsh buccaneer who led raids on Spanish towns in the Caribbean, sacked Panama in 1671 and later became governor of Jamaica.
henry-v-of-england: The young English king who revived the claim to France and beat a much larger French army at Agincourt in 1415.
hernan-cortes: The Spanish conquistador who landed in Mexico in 1519, allied with the Aztecs' enemies and overthrew their capital Tenochtitlan.
hestia: The Greek goddess of the hearth and the household fire, honoured first at every sacrifice and rarely seen in the tales.
horatio-nelson: The British admiral who won at the Nile and Copenhagen and died in the hour of victory at Trafalgar in 1805.
icarus: The boy who flew from Crete on wings of feathers and wax his father made, and fell into the sea when he climbed too near the sun.
jan-zizka: The one-eyed Bohemian commander who led the Hussites to victory with war wagons and gunfire against far larger armies in the 1420s.
jean-lafitte: The French-born privateer of the Gulf coast who ran a smuggling base near New Orleans and aided the American defence in 1815.
jotnar: The giants of Norse myth, older than the gods, who live beyond the walls of the world and often stand against Asgard.
khufu: The Egyptian pharaoh of the Fourth Dynasty who had the Great Pyramid built at Giza, tallest structure of its age.
kitsune: The fox spirit of Japanese folklore, which gains more tails with age and can take human shape to charm or trick people.
krampus: The horned, chain-rattling figure of Alpine folk custom who walks beside Saint Nicholas in early December to scare unruly children.
kublai-khan: The grandson of Genghis who completed the Mongol conquest of China, founded the Yuan dynasty and ruled from Khanbaliq.
la-befana: The old woman of Italian Epiphany tradition who flies on a broom on the eve of Epiphany, leaving gifts for children.
leif-erikson: The Norse sailor from Greenland who, according to the sagas, reached the shores of Vinland, in North America, around the year 1000.
leprechaun: The small cobbler of Irish folklore, said to guard a hidden crock of gold and to grant wishes only if caught.
leto: The Greek goddess who bore the twins Apollo and Artemis, wandering the world to find a place to give birth.
liu-bei: The Han relative who rose from poverty, swore brotherhood with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei and founded the state of Shu.
long-john-silver: The one-legged sea cook of Stevenson's tale, a genial and cunning pirate who sails as ship's cook to search for treasure.
manticore: The beast of Persian and Greek reports with a man's face, a lion's body and a scorpion's tail, said to devour its prey.
marcus-aurelius: The Roman emperor and Stoic thinker who spent much of his reign on the Danube frontier fighting the Marcomanni.
mark-antony: The Roman general who stood by Caesar, shared power with Octavian and joined Cleopatra before losing at Actium.
matthias-corvinus: The Hungarian king, called the Raven King, who built the professional Black Army and fought the Ottomans and the Habsburgs in the fifteenth century.
mehmed-the-conqueror: The Ottoman sultan who besieged Constantinople with great cannon and took it in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire.
menelaus: The Spartan king whose wife was taken to Troy, and who fought Paris in single combat before the walls in Homer's Iliad.
midas: The king of the myths whose wish that all he touched turn to gold became a curse he had to wash away.
minos: The legendary king of Crete, who kept the Minotaur in the labyrinth and became a judge of the dead.
moby-dick: The great white whale of Melville's novel, a vast and scarred sperm whale that drew Captain Ahab across the oceans.
mummy: The wrapped corpse of an ancient Egyptian, preserved in linen and resin, which Victorian storytellers imagined walking out of its tomb.
napoleon-bonaparte: The Corsican artillery officer who rose to rule France, won a run of campaigns across Europe and fell at Waterloo in 1815.
narcissus: The beautiful youth of Greek myth who fell in love with his own reflection in a pool and wasted away beside it.
nefertiti: The queen of Egypt at Amarna, wife of Akhenaten, known from her painted limestone bust and a prominent place in the court's art.
nero: The last emperor of the Julio-Claudian line, remembered for his stage performances, his building projects and a rule that ended in revolt.
oberon: The fairy king of Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, who quarrels with his queen and sends Puck to bewitch the sleepers.
oceanus: The Titan who in Greek tradition was the great river encircling the whole world, source of all the waters.
oda-nobunaga: The Japanese warlord of the Sengoku age who broke rival clans with massed guns and brought much of the country under one hand.
oedipus: The Theban king of Greek tragedy who answered the Sphinx's riddle and then learned the truth about his own birth.
oliver-cromwell: The English commander who drilled the disciplined Ironsides, won the civil war against the king and later ruled as Lord Protector.
orestes: The son of Agamemnon in Greek tragedy, who returns to avenge his father and is then pursued by the Furies.
owain-glyndwr: The Welsh leader who rose against English rule in 1400, was proclaimed Prince of Wales and fought a long war for independence.
pandora: The first woman in Hesiod's tale, who opened a jar and let loose the troubles of the world, leaving only hope inside.
paris: The Trojan prince whose taking of Helen began the war, and who shot the arrow that brought down Achilles.
penelope: The queen of Ithaca who held off her suitors for years and set the contest of Odysseus' bow to decide among them.
pericles: The Athenian statesman and general who led the city in its golden age, built the Parthenon and guided it into the Peloponnesian War.
perun: The Slavic god of thunder and lightning, chief of the pantheon, whose oak and axe stood for storm and justice.
philip-ii-of-macedon: The Macedonian king who built a new army around the long-spear phalanx, brought Greece under his rule and was killed in 336 BC.
phoenix: The legendary bird that burns on a pyre of spice and rises anew from its own ashes, as ancient writers told it.
pompey: The Roman general called the Great, who cleared the seas of pirates, won in the East and then fought Caesar for Rome.
priam: The aged king of Troy in Homer's Iliad, who sees his city besieged and goes by night to beg Achilles for his son's body.
proteus: The old sea god of Homer's Odyssey who guards Poseidon's seals and takes many shapes to avoid giving answers to those who seize him.
qilin: The gentle chimeric beast of Chinese tradition, with the body of a deer and scales, whose coming marked a wise reign.
qin-shi-huang: The king of Qin who conquered the rival states in 221 BC, became China's first emperor and was buried with an army of clay soldiers.
quasimodo: The deaf bell-ringer of Notre-Dame in Hugo's novel, outwardly feared but fiercely loyal to the girl he shelters.
queen-mab: The tiny fairy midwife of Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet speech, who rides over sleepers in a nutshell chariot and brings dreams.
rhea: The Titan mother of the first Olympians, who in Hesiod's tale hid her youngest son Zeus from his father.
richard-iii-of-england: The last Plantagenet king, who fell fighting in the thick of the battle at Bosworth Field in 1485.
rollo: The Viking chieftain who settled his followers on the lower Seine and became the first ruler of what grew into Normandy.
romulus-and-remus: The twin brothers of Roman legend, raised by a she-wolf, who set about founding a city until their quarrel divided them.
saladin: The Kurdish sultan who united Egypt and Syria, retook Jerusalem in 1187 and later faced Richard the Lionheart on the Third Crusade.
sargon-of-akkad: The Mesopotamian ruler who rose from humble origins, united the cities of Sumer and Akkad and built one of the first empires.
satyr: A goat-legged, horse-eared follower of Dionysus in Greek tradition, shown on vases dancing, drinking and chasing nymphs.
sawney-bean: The Scottish cave-dweller of legend, said to have lived with a large family on the coast and preyed on travellers.
seti-i: The Egyptian pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty who campaigned in Canaan and Syria, restoring the empire's reach and building at Abydos.
sinbad-the-sailor: The merchant of the Arabian Nights who tells of seven voyages, meeting giant birds, strange islands and monsters.
siren: A song-monster of Homer's Odyssey whose voice drew sailors toward the rocks until Odysseus sailed past with his ears stopped.
sisyphus: The cunning king of Corinth whom Homer places in the underworld, forever pushing a boulder up a hill that it rolls back down.
stingy-jack: The Irish trickster who bargained with the Devil and was refused by both heaven and hell, wandering on with a lantern.
sulla: The Roman general who marched on Rome, won the civil war, held the dictatorship and then stepped down.
sun-tzu: The ancient Chinese general and strategist traditionally credited with The Art of War, a short book on winning with careful planning.
talos: The bronze giant who patrolled Crete's coast three times a day, hurling rocks at ships until Medea ended him in the Argonautica.
tantalus: The Lydian king punished in the underworld, standing in water and beneath fruit that drew back whenever he reached for it.
tartarus: The deep abyss below the underworld in Greek myth, where the Titans were bound and wrongdoers were punished.
telemachus: The son of Odysseus, who grew from a boy waiting in Ithaca to a spearman fighting beside his father in the hall.
the-boggart: The ill-tempered household spirit of northern England that sours milk, hides things and plagues families who name it.
the-brethren-of-the-rose-cross: The secret brotherhood of learned alchemists announced in early seventeenth-century pamphlets, whose existence was much debated and never proved.
the-brownie: The small helpful house spirit of Scotland who does chores by night in return for a bowl of cream and flees if thanked.
the-changeling: The fairy child left in a human cradle in place of a stolen baby, a figure from old folk belief across Europe.
the-colossus-of-rhodes: The vast bronze statue of the sun god Helios that overlooked the harbour of Rhodes, said in the tale to have stood astride the harbour.
the-domovoy: The house spirit of Slavic folk belief, an old man who lives by the hearth and guards the family if respected.
the-druids: The priests and sages of the ancient Celts, known from Roman writers as teachers, judges and keepers of sacred groves.
the-dryad: The tree nymph of Greek tradition, whose life is bound to a single tree and who dies if it is cut down.
the-empusa: The shape-shifting spirit sent by Hecate in Greek tradition, appearing in terrifying forms to frighten travellers.
the-forty-thieves: The band of robbers in the Arabian Nights tale who hide their treasure in a cave opened by a spoken command.
the-headless-queen-of-the-tower: The ghost said to walk the Tower of London, a queen carrying her head beneath her arm.
the-hoe-giant: A towering farm-bred brute of the Pit who swings a great field tool as a weapon and climbs the pitborn ladder.
the-huldra: The forest spirit of Scandinavian folklore who appears as a beautiful woman with a cow's tail and lures lonely wanderers.
the-maenads: The frenzied women who followed Dionysus in Greek myth, roaming the mountains in wild dance and tearing apart whatever they met.
the-medmenham-monks: The cloaked company of an eighteenth-century English club that met in a ruined abbey on the Thames and kept its rites secret.
the-moorland-coven: A band of witches who gather on the high western moors, an original creation with no source in any older tale.
the-myling: A child ghost of Scandinavian folklore, an unbaptised infant left to die that waits on the roads begging to be carried to a grave.
the-nymph: The young female nature spirit of Greek tradition who haunts springs, groves and mountains and attends the gods.
the-old-man-of-the-sea: The frail-looking stranger of Sinbad's fifth voyage who climbs onto his shoulders and refuses to let go, until Sinbad tricks him.
the-onryo: A vengeful ghost of Japanese folklore, a spirit wronged in life that returns with long black hair to haunt those who harmed it.
the-penanggalan: The flying-head spirit of Malay folklore, a woman whose head drifts free from her body at night and haunts childbirth.
the-pixie: The small, mischievous sprite of Cornwall and Devon who leads travellers astray and dances in rings on the moors.
the-poltergeist: The noisy spirit of European folklore that throws objects, slams doors and unsettles households without ever being seen.
the-revenant: A corpse that rises from the grave to trouble the living, as told in medieval chronicles of the northern lands.
the-roc: The giant bird of the Sinbad voyages, so huge that it carried off elephants and sailors landed upon its egg.
the-strigoi: The restless dead of Romanian folklore, said to rise from the grave at night and trouble their own families and villages.
the-three-brawlers: The three mighty men of Goethe's Faust, hired by the emperor's side to batter a rival army in the mountains.
the-tuatha-de-danann: The race of Irish myth who came to Ireland before the Gaels and brought treasures of power, including a cauldron, spear and sword.
the-weird-sisters: The three witches of Shakespeare's Macbeth, who meet the general on the heath and greet him with prophecies of kingship.
the-yurei: A faint Japanese ghost in the white burial kimono, with trailing hair and no feet, tied to the place of its death.
timur-tamerlane: The lame Turco-Mongol conqueror who built a vast empire from Samarkand and campaigned from Delhi to Anatolia in the late fourteenth century.
titania: The fairy queen of Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, who falls under a spell during her quarrel with Oberon.
titans: The elder race of Greek gods, children of Sky and Earth, who ruled before the Olympians overthrew them.
tokugawa-ieyasu: The warlord who won at Sekigahara in 1600 and founded the shogunate that ruled Japan in peace for over two hundred years.
toyotomi-hideyoshi: The farmer's son who rose through Nobunaga's ranks, finished the unification of Japan and built the great castle at Osaka.
trajan: The Roman emperor who conquered Dacia and pushed the empire to its widest reach, his deeds carved on a great column in Rome.
tutankhamun: The boy pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty, whose tomb survived almost untouched and was found in the Valley of the Kings in 1922.
unicorn: The one-horned beast of old natural histories and bestiaries, swift and wild and said to be taken only by cunning.
uranus: The primordial sky of Greek myth, husband of Earth and father of the Titans, overthrown by his own son Kronos.
veles: The Slavic god of cattle, waters and the underworld, who in the old tales steals from Perun and is chased by his thunder.
walter-raleigh: The Elizabethan courtier, soldier and explorer who sponsored colonies in Virginia and was finally beheaded under James I in 1618.
wellington: The Duke of Wellington, the British commander who drove the French from Spain and beat Napoleon at Waterloo in 1815.
will-o-the-wisp: The pale light that drifts over bogs and marshes in European folklore and leads night travellers off the safe path.
william-kidd: The Scottish-born captain hired to hunt pirates who was accused of turning pirate himself and was hanged in London in 1701.
william-marshal: The landless knight who rose through the tournaments to serve five English kings and ruled as regent for the boy Henry III.
william-the-conqueror: The Duke of Normandy who crossed the Channel in 1066, won at Hastings and was crowned King of England.
winged-victory: The winged goddess of victory in Greek tradition, shown alighting on warships and carrying the crown to the winner.
wu-zetian: The Tang concubine who rose to rule China in her own name, founding a short dynasty and governing for some fifteen years.
wyvern: The two-legged winged dragon with a barbed tail found in medieval heraldry, a common emblem on banners and shields.
xerxes-i: The Persian king who led a huge army and fleet into Greece in 480 BC, burned Athens and was beaten at Salamis.
yamata-no-orochi: The eight-headed, eight-tailed serpent of Japanese myth, slain by the storm god Susanoo to save a family's last daughter.
yggdrasil: The great ash at the centre of Norse myth, whose roots and branches reach through all the worlds.
zheng-he: The Ming admiral who led great treasure fleets across the Indian Ocean, reaching as far as East Africa between 1405 and 1433.
zhuge-liang: The brilliant adviser to Liu Bei in the Three Kingdoms era, famed for clever strategy, careful government and the northern campaigns of Shu.
